The coming population implosion

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...........the world is facing a population implosion by the end of teh century

Unique Selling Point:
Fresh new research, important to all of us.

Summary:
Continued global population growth through the century is no longer the most likely trajectory for the world's population. By contrast, world population might peak just after mid-century and substantially decline by 2100. Since 1950, the total global fertility rate has dropped by half (reasons – better education for women, lower child mortality, access to contraception, increased societal prosperity, economic uncertainty, unaffordable housing, etc). Though the global population is currently rising — mostly due to high fertility rates in African countries — experts have also observed falling fertility rates around the world. Replacement fertility is around 2.1 children per woman. The US, Denmark, China, and Singapore all have low fertility rates: 1.87, 1.73, 1.6, and 0.81, respectively. Japan, one of the most extreme cases of population implosion, has a fertility rate of 1.41. Its population has been declining for the past few years. This is concerning for demographers and economists because countries must hit what's known as "replacement fertility" in order to keep their populations — and their economies — stable.



Further information:
Continued global population growth through the century is no longer the most likely trajectory for the world's population. By contrast, world population might peak just after mid-century and substantially decline by 2100. Since 1950, the total global fertility rate has dropped by half (reasons – better education for women, lower child mortality, access to contraception, increased societal prosperity, economic uncertainty, unaffordable housing, etc). Though the global population is currently rising — mostly due to high fertility rates in African countries — experts have also observed falling fertility rates around the world. Replacement fertility is around 2.1 children per woman. The US, Denmark, China, and Singapore all have low fertility rates: 1.87, 1.73, 1.6, and 0.81, respectively. Japan, one of the most extreme cases of population implosion, has a fertility rate of 1.41. Its population has been declining for the past few years. This is concerning for demographers and economists because countries must hit what's known as "replacement fertility" in order to keep their populations — and their economies — stable.

South Africa Total Fertility Rate
• 1960 -- 6,04
• 1994 -- 4,98
• 2018 – 2,43
• 2020 – 2,26

The UN says Bulgaria is actually the world’s fastest shrinking nation, with its current population of about 7 million people expected to dwindle to 5.4 million by 2050 and 3.9 million by the end of the century.

This is concerning for demographers and economists because countries must hit what's known as "replacement fertility" in order to keep their populations — and their economies — stable.
• By 2050, 151 countries were forecasted to have a TFR lower than the replacement level (TFR <2·1),
• 183 were forecasted to have a TFR lower than replacement by 2100.
• 23 countries in the reference scenario, including Japan, Thailand, and Spain, were forecasted to have population declines greater than 50% from 2017 to 2100;
• China's population was forecasted to decline by 48·0% (−6·1 to 68·4).

Interviewees:
Prof Stein Emil Vollset – the University of Washington in Seattle
Prof Nicole de Wet-Billings, Wits
Prof Tom Moultrie, UCT
Prof Nancy Stiegler,UWC

---------------------------------------------------

A decline in the global population, an issue that may seem trivial now, is set to become a crucial policy concern in the years to come. Researchers say the fertility rate crash will have major global impacts - a shift the world is not currently prepared for.
Researchers at the University of Washington’s Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation recently published a study that predicts major change for the world as we know it. In around 2064, the global population will begin shrinking.
At first glance this may seem like a positive — studies show population growth is a driver of climate change and fewer people should mean more resources to go around. However, researchers say the world is ill-prepared for the “jaw-dropping” impact it will have.
THE FINDINGS OF THE STUDY
The research, published in the Lancet, focused on declining fertility rates (the average number of children a woman gives birth to). If the fertility rate in a country falls below approximately 2.1, the population will drop.
In 2017 the fertility rate was 2.4 — a drop of almost half from the rate of 4.7 in 1950. That number is expected to fall below 1.7 by 2100 causing a major population decline. Researchers predict the population will peak at 9.7 billion in 2064, dropping thereafter to 8.8 billion by the end of the century.
“I think it’s incredibly hard to think this through and recognise how big a thing this is; it’s extraordinary, we’ll have to reorganise societies,” said researcher Christopher Murray in a BBC News interview.
WHAT WILL THE WORLD LOOK LIKE IN 2100?
The list of most populated countries will look slightly different by the end of the century. China, currently topping the list with the largest population, will see a population decline of almost a half. India will take its place with a population of 1.09 billion, followed by Nigeria at 791 million.
23 countries will see their population decline by more than 50%, including Spain, Thailand, and Japan. Out of 195 countries across the world, 183 will have a fertility rate lower than 2.1 by 2100, making this a profoundly global problem.
South Africa will not be bucking this trend. The country is already below the global average with a fertility rate of 2.29 in 2017, and that will drop to 1.7 in the coming years. The study forecasts a peak of the population in 2073 at 78 million, thereafter dropping to 74 million.
Age structures will shift along with declining populations. The number of children under five will fall from 681 million to 401 million, while the over-80 population will increase six-fold to 866 million.
WHAT IMPACT DOES A DECLINING POPULATION HAVE?
“A sustained total fertility rate (TFR) lower than the replacement level in many countries, including China and India, would have economic, social, environmental, and geopolitical consequences.”
“Our forecasts for a shrinking global population have positive implications for the environment, climate change, and food production, but possible negative implications for labour forces, economic growth, and social support systems in parts of the world with the greatest fertility declines.”
An inverted age structure — where there are more older people than young – brings several negative consequences. It is unclear how health care systems will manage, whether the current tax structures will survive and whether people over 65 will be able to retire at all.
Currently, there is no clear solution. Countries are looking to migration, enhanced maternity and paternity leave, free childcare, and financial incentives as avenues to improve fertility rates, but their efficacy is unknown.
Researchers say this will cause incredible social change and is likely to become a crucial policy concern in the years to come.

Script:


V/O:
When most people think of the future of humanity on Earth, they see an overpopulated planet, with billions of people trapped in in mega cities, competing for scarce resources……. But this commonly held doomsday scenario may not be the last word on the world’s population figures.
18,5
LINK:
A new study has attracted a lot of worldwide attention because of its startling predictions that contradict what is commonly believed about the future numbers of humans on earth.
V/O:
Tom Moultrie Professor of Demography at the centre for actuarial research at the University of Cape Town says that demographers have abandoned the prediction of uncontrolled population growth some time ago.
14
Tom:
From the 1960’s, seventies and eighties there was this global concern over over population. We’ve all realized that that kind of ongoing explosion is certainly not going to happen indefinitely.
V/O:
The new study develops this idea and concludes that instead of a population explosion at the end of this century, the earth can look forward to a population implosion of staggering proportions.

They predict that many countries including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Thailand and Italy will see their numbers diminish by at least half. And a country like Latvia is predicted to lose seventy eight percent of its population.

Prof Nicole De Wet-Billings of Wits says the study is important because it also incorporates novel variables in their modelling.
13


15


8
Nicole:
What really struck me was the contention that education and contraceptive use will change what our population l0oks like by 2100. And I think in many ways it is underplayed how important it is to educate females, how important it is to give them access to family planning and contraception.
V/O:
The comprehensive report includes data from 195 countries and shows clearly that population decline is accelerating, says Prof Stein Emil Vollset, the lead author of the study who teaches in the USA.

19
Vollset:
If we go back to 1950, there were less than 5 countries in the world that had a declining population. Now there are a hundred countries.
V/O:
And more will be joining the list throughout the century. One of the key factors in population decline is replacement fertility rate.
9
Nicole:
So, replacement fertility is two children per woman. Essentially, she is replacing herself and her partner in the population. When fertility fall below that, it oes tend to be worrisome.
Vollset:
It is a rule of thumb that the number of children born to women is less than 2.1, then the population will in the long run decline.
V/O:
And all over the world, fertility rates are declining. For example, in South Africa the fertility rate in the nineteen fifties was 6 point 5 children per woman. Today it is down to two point 4 children.

Prof Nancy Stiegler, a demographer at the University of the Western Cape says better socio-economic conditions and general increased prosperity worldwide provides an impetus for the decline.
16


11
Nancy:
We see that when people have better access to health, when they have obviously have better access to contraceptive and reproductive health, we see that fertility is declining. On top of this education is also playing a huge role. By educating girls you are usually slowing down fertility.
V/O:
Rapid urbanization also plays a role in lowering the number of children per woman. In cities there is less space and the high cost of living results in smaller families. Brain drain, and emigration to countries with more opportunities, are also major drivers in many instances.
25
LINK:
The implications of fewer people on earth one day are staggering.
V/O:
A first consequence is that population aging will become major factor. We already see this in Japan.
7
Nancy:
Right now half of the population is less than fifty years old, but half the population is over fifty years old.
V/O:
And this means fewer economically active people in a society who can keep the economy going and pay taxes. It also means more elderly people with health and social issues straining financial resources. And an ever-shrinking workforce can in the end cripple economies.

China is one of the countries which will be severely affected.
21
Volsett:
For the country with the largest population today, China, we don’t see 50 percent decrease, but almost. Down to 730 million, I think.
V/O:
That is seven hundred million less people than those living in China today! And India will have about 4 hundred million fewer people.

However, some developed countries with very low fertility rates buck the trend. The fertility rates in Australia, Sweden, Canada and Germany are well below two point one, but they have maintained and even increased their population numbers through immigration.

AND the report highlights a glaring exception to the trend. It predicts tha, Africa’s population will not decrease, but actually increase massively towards the year 2100.
8


16,5



11
Volsett:
Than constitutes an increase of two billion n Sub-Sahara Africa from one to three billion.
V/O:
That is an astounding number, and it is because women in Sub-Saharan Africa in general have between 4 and five children. However, South Africa does not follow this trend and has a fairly low fertility rate.
15,5
Nicole:
So, Southern Africa is quite unique and this is attributed to education, contraceptive use.
Tom:
For South Africa projections are that our population will carry on growing to roughly about 2070 or 2080 and will porbalbly hit some maximum of between 75 and eighty million. So another 20 million people in South Africa.
V/O:
Our population will stabilize at this level, and then slowly decline towards the end of the century.

But after the rapid population growth in Africa, populations there will also follow the trend and decline into the 22nd century, resulting in a much smaller world population.
7

11
V/O:
The study’s projections could assist South Africa to plan ahead for twenty million more people in terms of schools, and housing and infra structure.

And with shrinking and aging populations in Europe and Asia, attracting young and qualified immigrants from Africa could even result in bidding wars.
9

9
LINK:
The environment will also benefit greatly from fewer people on earth.
Vollset:
Of course a population decline is in some respect bad news, but it is also good news because it is less stress on the planet, less strsss on food production, less stress on fisheries, and it will not hurt climate
LINK:
There is a big question to be answered , is the a planet prepared for the coming population implosion?
Vollset:
I think we are not prepared. And it is not only implosion, it is also the very strong population growth that we project for Africa, so there are huge challenges ahead of us. And of course, we can also ask the question, “How many people should we be on this planet.

Derek:
Good question

Vollset:
Do we want to grow forever? Probably not.

metadata.Summary: Continued global population growth through the century is no longer the most likely trajectory for the world's population. By contrast, world population might peak just after mid-century and substantially decline by 2100. Since 1950, the total global fertility rate has dropped by half (reasons – better education for women, lower child mortality, access to contraception, increased societal prosperity, economic uncertainty, unaffordable housing, etc). Though the global population is currently rising — mostly due to high fertility rates in African countries — experts have also observed falling fertility rates around the world. Replacement fertility is around 2.1 children per woman. The US, Denmark, China, and Singapore all have low fertility rates: 1.87, 1.73, 1.6, and 0.81, respectively. Japan, one of the most extreme cases of population implosion, has a fertility rate of 1.41. Its population has been declining for the past few years. This is concerning for demographers and economists because countries must hit what's known as "replacement fertility" in order to keep their populations — and their economies — stable.

This is concerning for demographers and economists because countries must hit what's known as "replacement fertility" in order to keep their populations — and their economies — stable. • By 2050, 151 countries were forecasted to have a TFR lower than the replacement level (TFR <2·1), • 183 were forecasted to have a TFR lower than replacement by 2100. • 23 countries in the reference scenario, including Japan, Thailand, and Spain, were forecasted to have population declines greater than 50% from 2017 to 2100; • China's population was forecasted to decline by 48·0% (−6·1 to 68·4). Interviewees: Prof Stein Emil Vollset – the University of Washington in Seattle Prof Nicole de Wet-Billings, Wits Prof Tom Moultrie, UCT Prof Nancy Stiegler,UWC --------------------------------------------------- A decline in the global population, an issue that may seem trivial now, is set to become a crucial policy concern in the years to come. Researchers say the fertility rate crash will have major global impacts - a shift the world is not currently prepared for. Researchers at the University of Washington’s Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation recently published a study that predicts major change for the world as we know it. In around 2064, the global population will begin shrinking. At first glance this may seem like a positive — studies show population growth is a driver of climate change and fewer people should mean more resources to go around. However, researchers say the world is ill-prepared for the “jaw-dropping” impact it will have. THE FINDINGS OF THE STUDY The research, published in the Lancet, focused on declining fertility rates (the average number of children a woman gives birth to). If the fertility rate in a country falls below approximately 2.1, the population will drop. In 2017 the fertility rate was 2.4 — a drop of almost half from the rate of 4.7 in 1950. That number is expected to fall below 1.7 by 2100 causing a major population decline. Researchers predict the population will peak at 9.7 billion in 2064, dropping thereafter to 8.8 billion by the end of the century. “I think it’s incredibly hard to think this through and recognise how big a thing this is; it’s extraordinary, we’ll have to reorganise societies,” said researcher Christopher Murray in a BBC News interview. WHAT WILL THE WORLD LOOK LIKE IN 2100? The list of most populated countries will look slightly different by the end of the century. China, currently topping the list with the largest population, will see a population decline of almost a half. India will take its place with a population of 1.09 billion, followed by Nigeria at 791 million. 23 countries will see their population decline by more than 50%, including Spain, Thailand, and Japan. Out of 195 countries across the world, 183 will have a fertility rate lower than 2.1 by 2100, making this a profoundly global problem. South Africa will not be bucking this trend. The country is already below the global average with a fertility rate of 2.29 in 2017, and that will drop to 1.7 in the coming years. The study forecasts a peak of the population in 2073 at 78 million, thereafter dropping to 74 million. Age structures will shift along with declining populations. The number of children under five will fall from 681 million to 401 million, while the over-80 population will increase six-fold to 866 million. WHAT IMPACT DOES A DECLINING POPULATION HAVE? “A sustained total fertility rate (TFR) lower than the replacement level in many countries, including China and India, would have economic, social, environmental, and geopolitical consequences.” “Our forecasts for a shrinking global population have positive implications for the environment, climate change, and food production, but possible negative implications for labour forces, economic growth, and social support systems in parts of the world with the greatest fertility declines.” An inverted age structure — where there are more older people than young – brings several negative consequences. It is unclear how health care systems will manage, whether the current tax structures will survive and whether people over 65 will be able to retire at all. Currently, there is no clear solution. Countries are looking to migration, enhanced maternity and paternity leave, free childcare, and financial incentives as avenues to improve fertility rates, but their efficacy is unknown. Researchers say this will cause incredible social change and is likely to become a crucial policy concern in the years to come.
